analysis.one_liner: Requires large employers to offer and help pay for family health insurance for their workers.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and died in House subcommittees in 2000 without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a new section to the federal wage-and-hour law requiring every employer with 50 or more workers to offer a family health plan at least as good as the standard Blue Cross-Blue Shield plan available to federal employees, and to pay the same share of the premium the government pays for that plan. Workers would pay their share through payroll deduction, and contract workers would count as employees. It also dealt with people already covered by Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee insurance, or military family coverage. It never advanced past committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large employers and their families, especially the uninsured, would gain guaranteed access to employer-based family coverage with a mandatory employer contribution toward the premium.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at large employers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Every employer with 50 or more full-time employees would have to offer each employee a family health plan with benefits at least equal to the Blue Cross-Blue Shield Standard Plan in the Federal Employees Health Benefit Program as of January 1, 2000.
Employers would have to contribute at least the same share of the premium the federal government pays for that plan, with a prorated contribution for part-time workers between 10 and 30 hours a week.
Coverage would have to begin within 30 days of hire, and contract workers would be treated as employees, closing a common way of avoiding coverage obligations.
Employers that failed to comply would face civil money penalties and enforcement actions by the Secretary of Labor.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers would bear a new premium contribution for employees and their families. Health insurers would gain a large mandated market. Workers would pay their premium share through withholding, and workers already on Medicare, Medicaid, federal employee coverage, or military family coverage would be required to take the employer plan or have the federal program pay their premium share.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers, workers, and federal health programs

drawbacks.text: A mandate on employers with 50 or more workers creates a new cost per employee, which employers could pass on through lower wages or slower hiring, a standard concern with employer-mandated benefits.

The bill would require workers already covered by Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, or CHAMPUS to accept the employer plan or have the federal program pay their premium share, shifting costs among workers, employers, and federal programs rather than simply adding coverage.
No employer contribution is required for employees working fewer than 10 hours a week, leaving the lowest-hour workers uncovered.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 44 million uninsured Americans the bill cites, a guaranteed employer plan with a fixed employer contribution would have been a substantial gain, and the bill's design (modeled on an existing, well-regarded federal plan) was straightforward. The real costs fall on large employers and partly on federal programs, and low-hour workers would be left out. It was a broad employer mandate, not a free benefit, but the trade-off clearly favored coverage over cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees and several subcommittees in early 2000, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the Health Care for Working Families Act of 2000 on January 24, 2000, with no cosponsors.

The Speaker referred it to five committees at once — Education and the Workforce, Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services — a split referral that requires agreement across many jurisdictions before a bill can move.

In February 2000 it was sent to subcommittees on Health, Health and Environment, Military Personnel, Civil Service, Employer-Employee Relations, and Workforce Protections, and the Department of Defense was asked for its views; no committee or subcommittee ever reported it out.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, with the bill never having reached a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers kept the status quo: no new obligation to offer or help pay for family health coverage, and no exposure to the bill's civil penalties. Health insurers gained no new mandated market of employees at large firms. Uninsured workers and their families gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; no colleagues signed on as cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 24, 2000 and referred it to its Health Subcommittee, but never held a markup or reported it out.

against.name: House committees on Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform, and Armed Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill under a split, five-committee referral and took no action to advance it during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only supporter was a single Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split on the merits is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to offer a family health plan and pay the federal government's share of the premium for every employee, including contract workers, with civil money penalties for noncompliance. Because the bill died, these employers kept bearing none of that cost.

The bill would have routed millions of newly covered workers into private employer plans benchmarked to a private plan in the federal employees' program, creating a large mandated market for insurers and locking in employer-based private coverage as the channel for health benefits.

industries.industry: Federal health programs (Medicare, Medicaid, FEHBP, CHAMPUS)
industries.note: Enrollees in these programs would have had to take employer coverage where offered, moving some people off public coverage, but where they did not, the federal program would have to pay the employee's premium share, adding a new cost to those programs and the taxpayers who fund them.
